## Why this training

::: {.lead}
Companies will **build AI apps and agents**, then connect them to their own systems.
:::

Those connections give agents access to company tools, data and services.

::: {.takeaway}
This event teaches teams how to **deploy those applications safely**.
:::

::: {.notes}
Many companies on the platform will do more than use hosted models and datasets.
They will build applications and agent workflows around them. The event focuses
on the practical gap between building an application and deploying it safely.
:::

## The risk behind the demo

::: {.statement}
A compromised agent can use the **permissions its deployer gave it**.
:::

::: {.takeaway}
The potential damage depends on **what the agent can access**.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the central idea linking the session's security topics. In the proposed
scenario, an attacker uses a tool response to influence an agent that already
has access to the company's systems. The attacker does not need to hold the
agent's credentials directly. The impact depends on the agent's actual
permissions and the controls around its tools and runtime.
:::

## Two deliverables, one demo environment

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
### Conference session

A demo-led session, delivered live or as a recorded video.

Show an attack, then show the mitigation.
:::

::: {.column}
### Take-home pack

A repository participants can clone and work through independently.

Reproduce the demo and practise the fixes.
:::
::::

::: {.takeaway}
Build the **sandboxed emulator once** and use it in both.
:::

# The conference session {.section-title background-color="#101a2b"}

A visible attack, a tested mitigation, and the controls behind it.

## One agent, two configurations

The demo switches the same agent from `unsafe` to `hardened`.

::: {.steps}
1. **Run the attack** and observe the impact.
2. **Try the obvious fix** and show where it falls short.
3. **Apply the hardened configuration** and test the attack again.
:::

::: {.takeaway}
Make the changes to **permissions and isolation** visible.
:::

::: {.notes}
Keep the agent and demonstration files consistent so the audience can compare
the two configurations. The flag selects concrete controls in the emulator.
Explain those controls rather than presenting the flag as a general guarantee
of security. Monitoring makes the difference between the runs visible.
:::

## The simulated attack chain

::: {.steps .compact}
1. **Poisoned tool response:** an MCP tool returns a hidden instruction.
2. **Code execution:** the agent runs attacker code in its container.
3. **Container escape:** the scenario crosses the container boundary.
4. **Wider access:** the agent reaches mock secrets or an internal service.
5. **Persistence:** a memory write influences a later session.
:::

::: {.notes}
The chain is a proposed scenario inside the local, sandboxed company emulator.
Use simulated systems and data, with no Pharos infrastructure in scope. The
exact target for step 4 still needs to be chosen. A container escape depends
on a specific vulnerability or misconfiguration and is not an automatic
consequence of prompt injection. Distinguish simulated steps from real
exploits when presenting the demo.
:::

## Two views of the same run

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
### What the user sees

A calm, helpful chat response.

The task appears to complete normally.
:::

::: {.column}
### What the trace reveals

The actual tool calls and data access.

The boundary crossed and systems reached.
:::
::::

::: {.takeaway}
The live trace and access map show **what the chat leaves out**.
:::

::: {.notes}
Use a live instrument panel over the running agent, reading its trace log.
Keep the renderer simple. Show the two views together and update the access
map as the simulated impact spreads. This is the visual centre of the demo.
:::

## A local company stack

::: {.lead}
Run the demo in a **sandboxed company environment**.
:::

::: {.steps}
1. Use a local Docker or Kubernetes setup familiar to the audience.
2. Simulate company data, services and attack targets.
3. Keep Pharos infrastructure outside the demonstration.
:::

::: {.notes}
The original proposal centred on the HPC platform. This version moves the
target to a generic company stack to make the demo easier to relate to and
avoid implying that the demonstration exposes a weakness in Pharos.
Explain that change of scope when discussing the proposal. Cluster-specific
attacks remain outside this event.
:::

## From the demo to deployment

:::: {.module-grid}
::: {.column .module}
### Security vocabulary
Map the demo to the relevant OWASP GenAI and LLM risks.
:::
::: {.column .module}
### Practical controls
Least privilege, secure tools, isolation and monitoring.
:::
::: {.column .module}
### Governance
Risk tiers, provider and deployer roles, and the EU AI Act.
:::
::: {.column .module}
### Deployment architecture
Trusted and untrusted zones, with controlled access between them.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
This is the less technical half of the session, intended to balance the demos
with governance and deployment practice. The frameworks should connect to
what participants just observed. Use the trace to discuss operational evidence
and record keeping. Verify any legal obligations and article references for
the specific system and role before presenting them as requirements.
:::

# The take-home pack {.section-title background-color="#101a2b"}

The same demo, with guided practice and deeper implementation detail.

## What participants clone

::: {.steps}
1. **The agent:** compare the unsafe and hardened configurations.
2. **The trace renderer:** inspect the demo, then adapt it to their logs.
3. **The attack harness:** rerun the scenarios and assess their own agent.
:::

::: {.takeaway}
The pack turns the session into **hands-on practice**.
:::

::: {.notes}
The session is demo-led, so the take-home pack is where participants do the
exercises themselves. Include the depth that will not fit in the live slot.
The current 90-minute framing is provisional until the slot length is
confirmed. Explain the expected log format and scope of the harness so
participants know what they need to adapt for their own agents.
:::

## Six practical modules

:::: {.module-grid}
::: {.column .module}
### Sandboxing
Configure containers, gVisor, WASM and virtual machines.
:::
::: {.column .module}
### Secure tool design
Use narrow interfaces and validated arguments. Avoid raw shell access.
:::
::: {.column .module}
### Paths and permissions
Implement path canonicalisation and least privilege.
:::
::: {.column .module}
### Monitoring
Choose useful signals and alert thresholds.
:::
::: {.column .module}
### Sensitive data
Cover minimisation, redaction, residency and local processing.
:::
::: {.column .module}
### Deployment review
Use a checklist and an OWASP / AI Act self-assessment.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
This is where the topic list from the original proposal lives in full.
The session demonstrates the mechanism and the pack teaches the practice.
The self-assessment component connects to T3.6. Treat it as a learning aid
and verify the OWASP and AI Act references before publishing the pack.
:::

## A guided route through the pack

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
### Observe the failure

1. Run the attack.
2. Inspect the trace.
3. Try the obvious fix.
:::
::: {.column}
### Apply and test the controls

4. Apply the mitigation.
5. Read the walkthrough.
6. Assess the result.
:::
::::

::: {.takeaway}
Participants can complete the route **without attending the session**.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the grant framing: a repository that others can clone and work
through independently, with a route into the T3.6 self-assessment.
The guided path reuses the same artefacts rather than adding another
set of materials to build.
:::

# The proposal {.section-title background-color="#101a2b"}

Choose the deliverables and how the event fits the training programme.

## The decision

:::: {.columns .option-grid}
::: {.column}
### Session only

Lower build effort.

A demo-led introduction to the risks and controls.
:::
::: {.column}
### Pack only

Independent, repeatable learning.

No shared live demonstration.
:::
::: {.column .recommended}
### Both

The proposed approach.

One build supports the session and a reusable WP3 output.
:::
::::

::: {.takeaway}
**Event format:** standalone training or part of another event?
:::

::: {.notes}
Both is my preferred option. Confirm the relationship to the WP3 output
when agreeing the scope. Open questions: the step-4 attack target,
whether CING, CYENS or KIOS contribute to the build, the session length,
and the AI Act article references. The short note is due 23 September.
:::
